title: Shopping Basics: How Much Is It?
canDo: Can ask about prices and understand simple numbers and short, direct instructions in a shop.
goal: Ask how much things cost and understand simple price answers across all three pillars.

warmup.prompt: Show a picture of a market stall with price tags. Ask: What is your favourite food to buy at a market?
warmup.tutorAction: Give a short example: I buy apples. Let the student answer, even with one word.

theory.structure: How much is + singular noun? / How much are + plural noun? Answer: It is + price. / They are + price.
examples: How much is the bread? It is two euros.
How much are the apples? They are one euro fifty.
How much is the coffee? It is three dollars.
theory.method: Show the question formula with a singular and plural example. Ask concept-checking questions: Is bread singular or plural? Which verb do we use for apples? Then ask the student to ask about one item on the screen.
theory.checkQuestion: Do we say how much is the apples or how much are the apples?

comprehension.source: Read this short dialogue twice at a steady pace: Customer: Excuse me, how much is the milk? Shop worker: It is one pound twenty. Customer: And how much are the eggs? Shop worker: They are two pounds.
comprehension.factCheck: Ask: How much is the milk? (one pound twenty). How much are the eggs? (two pounds).
comprehension.toneCheck: Ask: Is the customer polite or rude? Accept a simple answer and ask the student to point to the word that shows politeness, such as Excuse me.

conversation.task: Shop role-play: the student is a customer and asks the tutor, who plays the shop worker, about three items on the screen. Then they swap roles. The student must ask at least two price questions.
conversation.mandate: Keep your talk time under 40 percent. Use the screen prices and praise each complete question before correcting anything.

title: Telling the Time and Making Plans
canDo: Can understand and ask about times and simple timetables for everyday activities.
goal: Say and ask what time something happens using at with times and simple time expressions.

warmup.prompt: Show a clock at half past eight. Ask: What time do you start work or school?
warmup.tutorAction: Model a short answer: I start at eight thirty. Let the student answer freely.

theory.structure: What time is it? It is + time. / The class starts at + time.
examples: What time is it? It is half past eight.
The class starts at nine o'clock.
The shop closes at six in the evening.
theory.method: Show the clock on screen and the question formula. Ask concept-checking questions: Do we use at before a time? What words describe half past? Then ask the student to say the time shown on the clock.
theory.checkQuestion: Do we say the class starts in nine or at nine?

comprehension.source: Read this timetable aloud twice at a steady pace: Bus 12 leaves at 7:15. Bus 14 leaves at 8:30. The last bus leaves at 10 at night.
comprehension.factCheck: Ask: When does Bus 12 leave? (7:15). When does the last bus leave? (10 at night).
comprehension.toneCheck: Ask: Is the timetable information urgent or routine? Accept a simple answer and ask the student to point to the word that shows timing, such as last.

conversation.task: Timetable question: the student asks the tutor about the bus times on screen, then they swap. The student must ask two questions using What time and reply with a time using at.
conversation.mandate: Keep your talk time under 40 percent. Use the screen timetable and praise each complete question.

mistakes: The bus leaves in eight thirty.

upgrades.accurate: The bus leaves in eight thirty.
upgrades.native: The bus leaves at half past eight.
What time does the class start?

title: Around Town: There Is and There Are
canDo: Can describe places in a town and give simple directions using basic prepositions.
goal: Describe what is in a place and where things are using there is, there are, and next to.

warmup.prompt: Show a street picture with a bank, a park, and a café. Ask: What is in your neighbourhood?
warmup.tutorAction: Point to the picture and give a short example: There is a park near my house. Let the student answer freely.

theory.structure: There is + singular noun / There are + plural noun + place (in, on, next to)
examples: There is a bank on the main street.
There are two cafés next to the park.
There is a bus stop near the school.
theory.method: Show the street picture with labels. Ask concept-checking questions: Is the noun singular or plural? Which form do we use with two cafés? Then ask the student to describe one place in the picture.
theory.checkQuestion: Do we say there is two cafés or there are two cafés?

comprehension.source: Read this description twice at a steady pace: In our town, there is a big library. There are three shops on the high street. The post office is next to the bank.
comprehension.factCheck: Ask: How many shops are on the high street? (three). What is next to the bank? (the post office).
comprehension.toneCheck: Ask: Does the speaker like the town? Accept a simple answer and ask the student to point to the word that shows the opinion, such as big.

conversation.task: Town guide: the student describes three places in the picture to the tutor using there is or there are, then gives directions from the bank to the café using next to.
conversation.mandate: Keep your talk time under 40 percent. Use the street picture on screen and praise each complete description before correcting.

mistakes: The café is next the park.

upgrades.accurate: The café is next the park.
upgrades.native: The café is next to the park.

title: Skills and Abilities: Can and Can't
canDo: Can talk about personal abilities and skills in simple sentences and understand short descriptions of them.
goal: Say what you can and cannot do using can and can't with a base verb.

warmup.prompt: Show a picture of someone swimming and someone cooking. Ask: Can you swim? Can you cook?
warmup.tutorAction: Model a short answer: I can swim, but I can't cook well. Let the student answer freely.

theory.structure: Subject + can / can't + base verb (no to, no s)
examples: I can speak two languages.
She can drive, but she can't ride a bike.
We can't come to the party on Friday.
theory.method: Show the formula with the two example types. Ask concept-checking questions: Which verb form follows can? Do we add s after she? Then ask the student to say one thing they can do and one they can't do.
theory.checkQuestion: Do we say she can drives or she can drive?

comprehension.source: Read this text twice at a steady pace: Tom is a very good cook. He can make pasta and soup. He can't swim, but he can run very fast.
comprehension.factCheck: Ask: What can Tom make? (pasta and soup). What can't Tom do? (swim). What can he do very fast? (run).
comprehension.toneCheck: Ask: Does Tom seem proud of his skills? Accept a simple answer and ask the student to point to the word that shows the feeling, such as very good.

conversation.task: Skills exchange: the student tells the tutor three things they can do and one thing they cannot do. The tutor asks one follow-up question: Can you show me?
conversation.mandate: Keep your talk time under 40 percent. Use the screen pictures to prompt the student, and praise each complete sentence.

title: Weather and Seasons: It Is Hot and It Is Cold
canDo: Can describe the weather and seasons using simple adjectives and understand a short forecast.
goal: Describe the weather and seasons using it is with simple adjectives.

warmup.prompt: Show a picture of a sunny beach and a snowy street. Ask: Which weather do you prefer?
warmup.tutorAction: Give a short example: I prefer sunny days. Let the student answer freely.

theory.structure: It is + adjective (hot, cold, rainy, windy, sunny) / In + season
examples: It is hot in summer.
It is cold and windy today.
In winter, it is often rainy.
theory.method: Show the weather adjectives with matching pictures. Ask concept-checking questions: Do we use it is for weather? Which season has snow? Then ask the student to describe today's weather using two adjectives.
theory.checkQuestion: Do we say the weather is hot or it weather is hot?

comprehension.source: Read this forecast twice at a steady pace: Tomorrow it will be sunny in the morning. In the afternoon, it will be windy and cold. There is a chance of rain in the evening.
comprehension.factCheck: Ask: What will the weather be in the morning? (sunny). What will the afternoon be like? (windy and cold). When is the chance of rain? (in the evening).
comprehension.toneCheck: Ask: Does the forecast sound good or bad for a day out? Accept a simple answer and ask the student to point to a word that shows it, such as chance.

conversation.task: Weather report: the student gives a short weather report for tomorrow to the tutor, using three adjectives, then describes their favourite season with it is.
phrases: I like it when it is ...
conversation.mandate: Keep your talk time under 40 percent. Use the weather pictures on screen and praise each complete report.

mistakes: The weather is very hot in summer and it is good.

upgrades.accurate: The weather is very hot in summer and it is good.
upgrades.native: It is very hot in summer, and I like it.

title: Yesterday Was Busy: Past Simple of To Be and Regular Verbs
canDo: Can describe past events and experiences using simple sentences about familiar topics.
goal: Describe yesterday using was, were, and regular past verbs.

warmup.prompt: Show a calendar with yesterday highlighted. Ask: What did you do yesterday?
warmup.tutorAction: Give a short example: I worked in the morning. Let the student answer freely.

theory.structure: I / he / she / it + was; we / you / they + were; verb + ed for regular verbs (worked, played)
examples: I was at home yesterday.
They were late for the meeting.
We worked in the garden and cooked lunch.
theory.method: Show the was and were forms with the regular past verb formula. Ask concept-checking questions: Which form follows they? Is worked a present or past form? Then ask the student to say one thing they did yesterday.
theory.checkQuestion: Do we say they was late or they were late?

comprehension.source: Read this text twice at a steady pace: Yesterday was a busy day for Ana. She was at work until five. Then she walked home and cooked dinner with her brother.
comprehension.factCheck: Ask: When was Ana at work? (until five). What did she do after work? (walked home and cooked dinner).
comprehension.toneCheck: Ask: Was Ana's day relaxed or busy? Accept a simple answer and ask the student to point to a word that shows it, such as busy.

conversation.task: Yesterday story: the student tells the tutor about yesterday in three sentences, using was or were in one and two regular past verbs. The tutor asks: What did you do after that?
conversation.mandate: Keep your talk time under 40 percent. Give the student time to finish each sentence and praise each complete past sentence.

title: Ordering Food: Would Like
canDo: Can order food, make polite requests, and understand a simple menu in a café or restaurant.
goal: Order food politely using would like and understand simple menu descriptions.

warmup.prompt: Show a café menu with three drinks and three snacks. Ask: What would you like to order today?
warmup.tutorAction: Give a short example: I would like a coffee, please. Let the student answer freely.

theory.structure: I / We / He / She would like + noun (or to + verb), please.
examples: I would like a sandwich, please.
She would like a cup of tea.
We would like to pay now.
theory.method: Show the would like formula and the menu. Ask concept-checking questions: Is would like polite or rude? Do we use to before a verb? Then ask the student to order one item from the menu.
theory.checkQuestion: After would like, do we use a noun or a verb with to?

comprehension.source: Read this dialogue twice at a steady pace: Waiter: What would you like? Customer: I would like the soup, please. Waiter: Would you like something to drink? Customer: Yes, I would like a glass of water.
comprehension.factCheck: Ask: What does the customer order first? (the soup). What does the customer order to drink? (a glass of water).
comprehension.toneCheck: Ask: Is the customer polite? Accept a simple answer and ask the student to point to the phrase that shows politeness, such as please.

conversation.task: Café role-play: the student is a customer and orders two items from the screen menu from the tutor, who plays the waiter. Then they swap roles. The waiter asks: Would you like anything else?
conversation.mandate: Keep your talk time under 40 percent. Use the menu on screen and praise each polite order before correcting anything.

mistakes: I want a coffee, please, and I would like the cake.
I would like go to pay.

upgrades.accurate: I want a coffee, please, and I would like the cake.
upgrades.native: I would like a coffee and the cake, please.

upgrades.accurate: I would like go to pay.

title: Feeling Unwell: Should and Shouldn't
canDo: Can give and understand simple advice about health, and describe common symptoms and needs.
goal: Describe a health problem and give simple advice using should and shouldn't.

warmup.prompt: Show a picture of a person with a headache. Ask: What should this person do?
warmup.tutorAction: Give a short example: They should rest. Let the student answer freely.

examples: You should drink more water when it is hot.
You shouldn't stay up late before a test.
She should see a doctor if the pain continues.
theory.method: Show the should and shouldn't formula. Ask concept-checking questions: Is it advice or a strong rule? Which verb form follows should? Then ask the student to give one piece of advice for the picture.
theory.checkQuestion: Do we say you should to drink or you should drink?

comprehension.source: Read this short health text twice at a steady pace: If you have a cold, you should rest and drink warm drinks. You shouldn't go to work if you have a fever. If the cough lasts more than a week, you should see a doctor.
comprehension.factCheck: Ask: What should you do with a cold? (rest and drink warm drinks). When shouldn't you go to work? (with a fever). When should you see a doctor? (if the cough lasts more than a week).
comprehension.toneCheck: Ask: Is the text giving strict orders or friendly advice? Accept a simple answer and ask the student to point to the word that shows it, such as should.

conversation.task: Health advice: the student describes a common problem (a headache, a sore throat, tiredness) to the tutor, who asks what they should do. The student gives two pieces of advice to the tutor using should or shouldn't.
conversation.mandate: Keep your talk time under 40 percent. Use the health picture on screen and praise each piece of advice before correcting.

mistakes: You shouldn't to drink coffee at night.

upgrades.accurate: You shouldn't to drink coffee at night.
upgrades.native: You shouldn't drink coffee at night.

title: At Work Right Now: Present Continuous
canDo: Can describe what people are doing now at work or in a familiar place using simple present continuous sentences.
goal: Describe actions happening now using am, is, or are with the -ing form.

warmup.prompt: Show a picture of an office with people working. Ask: What are the people doing right now?
warmup.tutorAction: Give a short example: The woman is typing an email. Let the student answer freely.

theory.structure: Subject + am / is / are + verb-ing (happening now or around now)
examples: I am writing a report at the moment.
He is talking on the phone.
They are having a meeting in the room.
theory.method: Show the formula with the office picture. Ask concept-checking questions: Is this happening now? Which form of to be follows he? Then ask the student to describe one person in the picture.
theory.checkQuestion: Do we say he is work or he is working?

comprehension.source: Read this text twice at a steady pace: It is ten o'clock at the hotel. The manager is checking the reservations. Two receptionists are answering the phones, and a cleaner is preparing the rooms.
comprehension.factCheck: Ask: What is the manager doing? (checking the reservations). What are the receptionists doing? (answering the phones).
comprehension.toneCheck: Ask: Does the text describe a calm or busy place? Accept a simple answer and ask the student to point to the phrase that shows it, such as are answering the phones.

conversation.task: Picture description: the student describes three people in the office picture to the tutor, using the present continuous. The tutor asks: What is the person next to them doing?
conversation.mandate: Keep your talk time under 40 percent. Use the office picture on screen and praise each complete description before correcting.

mistakes: She is work on the computer.

upgrades.accurate: She is work on the computer.
upgrades.native: She is working on the computer.

title: Holidays and Habits: Adverbs of Frequency
canDo: Can talk about holidays, habits, and routines using simple sentences and understand a short personal description.
goal: Describe how often you do things on holiday using always, usually, sometimes, and never.

warmup.prompt: Show a picture of a beach holiday. Ask: Do you go on holiday often?
warmup.tutorAction: Give a short example: I usually go to the beach in summer. Let the student answer freely.

theory.structure: Subject + adverb of frequency (always, usually, often, sometimes, never) + verb; adverb goes before the main verb but after am / is / are
examples: I always take a camera on holiday.
We usually visit the coast in summer.
She is never late for the train.
theory.method: Show the adverb scale from always to never. Ask concept-checking questions: Where does the adverb go with the verb to be? Where does it go with other verbs? Then ask the student to rank their holiday habits using two adverbs.
theory.checkQuestion: Where does never go in the sentence She is never late?

comprehension.source: Read this text twice at a steady pace: Mark usually goes on holiday in August. He always visits his family first. Sometimes he goes hiking, but he is never bored on the coast.
comprehension.factCheck: Ask: When does Mark usually go on holiday? (August). What does he always do first? (visit his family). What does he sometimes do? (go hiking).
comprehension.toneCheck: Ask: Does Mark enjoy his holidays? Accept a simple answer and ask the student to point to the phrase that shows it, such as never bored.

conversation.task: Holiday habits interview: the student tells the tutor how often they do four things on holiday (swim, take photos, cook, relax), using adverbs of frequency. The tutor asks one follow-up question: Why do you like that?
conversation.mandate: Keep your talk time under 40 percent. Use the beach picture on screen and praise each complete sentence before correcting.

mistakes: I go always to the beach.

upgrades.accurate: I go always to the beach.
upgrades.native: I always go to the beach.
